reported.title: delete_document performs no authorization check
reported.body: `delete_document` is reachable from `handle_delete_document` by any authenticated user and deletes by `id` with no admin check and no `owner_id` predicate. Any logged-in user can destroy any other user's documents by guessing or enumerating ids. `_assert_admin` is defined in this module but never called here.

reported.title: Admin check in purge_user is swallowed by bare except
reported.body: `_assert_admin` raises `Forbidden` for non-admins, but the call is wrapped in `try/except Exception: pass`, so the exception is discarded and execution continues to the `DELETE`. Any authenticated caller can therefore purge every document owned by an arbitrary `target_user_id`. A check that fails silently is equivalent to no check.

reported.title: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded development value
reported.body: `SECRET_KEY` previously failed fast at import time when `QUORUM_DEMO_SECRET` was unset. With `os.getenv(..., "dev-secret-change-me")`, a deployment that forgets to set the variable silently signs with a publicly known key. `sharing.sign()` / `resolve_share_link()` use this key, so anyone reading the repository can forge share-link signatures for arbitrary `doc_id` values and read documents they do not own.

reported.title: list_documents no longer clamps limit to MAX_PAGE_SIZE
reported.body: The clamp against `Config.MAX_PAGE_SIZE` was removed, so `handle_list_documents(token, limit=10_000_000)` is passed straight to the query. Any authenticated caller can force the whole documents table to be loaded into memory and serialised, a cheap denial-of-service. `MAX_PAGE_SIZE` is still defined in `Config` but is now unused.

reported.title: Path traversal: export filename joined without validation
reported.body: `export_path` joins the caller-supplied `filename` directly onto the user's export directory. `handle_export(token, doc_id, "../../etc/cron.d/x")` (or an absolute path, which `os.path.join` will make the whole result) escapes the export root and writes attacker-controlled JSON anywhere the process can write, including other users' export directories. Unlike `reports.write_report`, no `validators.export_name` normalisation is applied here.

reported.title: SSRF: user-supplied URL fetched with no scheme or host allowlist
reported.body: `fetch_remote_document` passes the caller's `url` straight to `requests.get` with no validation of scheme or host and with redirects followed by default. An authenticated user can point it at `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` or internal services (`http://localhost:6379/`, `file://`-style handlers via redirect), and the response body is returned to them in `body`, exfiltrating cloud credentials or internal data. Validate that the parsed scheme is http/https and that the resolved host is not private/loopback/link-local before fetching, and disable redirects or re-validate each hop.

reported.title: SQL injection: search term interpolated into query string
reported.body: `term` comes straight from the caller (`handle_search`) and is interpolated into the SQL text with an f-string and wrapped in single quotes. A term containing `'` terminates the literal, e.g. `x' OR 1=1 --` or `x' UNION SELECT id, password, 0, 0 FROM users --`, letting an authenticated user read arbitrary tables or bypass the `owner_id` restriction (which is itself interpolated rather than bound). Use bound parameters for `term` and `user["id"]`; only `column`, which is already resolved through the `SORTABLE` allowlist, may be interpolated.

reported.title: Mutable default argument accumulates scopes across share links
reported.body: `scopes: list = []` is evaluated once at function definition. When a caller omits `scopes` (as `handle_create_share` does), `scopes.append("read")` mutates the shared default. Worse, any caller that passes a list has that caller's list mutated too, and every subsequent default-argument call reuses the same object, so scopes granted on one share leak into later shares created with the default — silently widening permissions on links minted afterwards.

reported.title: TOCTOU between existence check and export write
reported.body: `os.path.exists(destination)` is checked, then the code deliberately sleeps 200 ms before opening the file with mode `"w"`. Two concurrent exports of the same filename (or an attacker who creates/symlinks the path during the sleep window) both pass the check and the second silently truncates and overwrites the first. The sleep widens the race to a trivially winnable size. Open with `os.open(destination, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL)` so creation and the existence check are atomic, and drop the sleep.

reported.title: Share signature compared with non-constant-time ==
reported.body: The HMAC/signature check uses `!=`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. Because `resolve_share_link` is callable repeatedly with attacker-chosen `signature` values, the timing difference can be used to recover a valid signature byte by byte. Use `secrets.compare_digest`, which is already importable here.

reported.title: Share links never expire: TTL stored but never checked
reported.body: `expires_at` is set to the raw TTL in seconds (`ttl or DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS`), not an absolute timestamp, and it is written to the `expires_in` column. `resolve_share_link` selects only `doc_id, scopes` and never compares anything against the current time, so every share link is valid forever. Store an absolute expiry (`time.time() + ttl`) and reject rows whose expiry has passed in `resolve_share_link`.

reported.title: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded development value
reported.body: `SECRET_KEY` previously came only from the environment and failed fast at import time when missing; it now silently defaults to the publicly known string `"dev-secret-change-me"`. reported.title: list_documents no longer clamps limit to MAX_PAGE_SIZE
reported.body: The clamp `min(int(limit), Config.MAX_PAGE_SIZE)` was removed, so the caller-supplied `limit` flows straight into the query. `handle_list_documents` exposes this to any authenticated caller, who can pass `limit=100000000` and force the server to materialise the whole table into a list of dicts — an easy unauthenticated-cost / memory-exhaustion lever. `Config.MAX_PAGE_SIZE` is now unused. reported.title: Export filename is joined unvalidated, allowing path traversal
reported.body: `export_path` joins the caller-supplied `filename` straight onto the per-user export directory with no normalisation or containment check. A filename such as `../../etc/cron.d/job` or an absolute path (`os.path.join` discards the prefix when the second component is absolute) resolves outside the user's directory, and `export_document` then opens it for writing with attacker-controlled JSON content. Any authenticated caller can reach this via `handle_export`. Compare `reports.write_report`, which sanitises through `validators.export_name`, and `indexer.extract_text`, which performs a `commonpath` containment check.

reported.title: SSRF: user-supplied URL fetched with no scheme or host allowlist
reported.body: `fetch_remote_document` passes the caller-controlled `url` directly to `requests.get` with no validation of scheme or host and with redirects enabled by default. An authenticated user can point the import at internal addresses — `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`, `http://127.0.0.1:6379/`, or `file://`-style handlers via redirect — and the full response body is returned to them as the imported document's `body`. This exposes cloud instance metadata and internal services. The URL must be parsed and both the scheme (`http`/`https` only) and resolved host validated against an allowlist / private-range denylist, with redirects disabled or re-validated.

reported.title: SQL injection: search term interpolated into query via f-string
reported.body: `search()` builds the SQL statement with an f-string that embeds the caller-supplied `term` (and `user["id"]`) directly into the query text: `... AND documents_fts MATCH '{term}'`. A term containing a single quote terminates the literal, so any authenticated caller can inject arbitrary SQL, e.g. `term="' OR 1=1 --"` returns every row in the table (bypassing the `owner_id` restriction), and more elaborate payloads can attach/read other tables. The `suggest()` function right below shows the parameterised form that should be used here. Note `column` is safe because it comes from the `SORTABLE` allowlist.

reported.title: Mutable default argument accumulates scopes across calls
reported.body: `scopes: list = []` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every caller that omits `scopes` shares the same list object. The first call appends `"read"` to it; that mutation persists, and because callers that *do* pass a list also get it mutated in place, the shared default silently accumulates whatever scopes are appended over the process lifetime. Combined with `handle_create_share` (which calls the no-arg form), share links minted later can carry scopes granted to an earlier, unrelated share — a privilege escalation on the recipient side, not just a style issue.

reported.title: Share signature compared with != instead of a constant-time compare
reported.body: `resolve_share_link` verifies the HMAC-style signature with a plain `!=` string comparison, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. An attacker who knows a `doc_id` can measure response timing to recover a valid signature byte by byte and then resolve a share link they were never given. `secrets` is already imported in this module, so `secrets.compare_digest` is available.

reported.title: Share links never expire and stored scopes are ignored on resolve
reported.body: `create_share_link` stores `expires_at = (ttl or DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS)` — a relative duration, with no creation timestamp recorded — and `resolve_share_link` never reads the expiry column at all. Consequently every share link is valid forever, defeating the advertised TTL. The same function selects `scopes` from the shares row and then discards it, returning the entire document row (`SELECT *`) regardless of what the link was scoped to, so a read-only share grants full record access. Store an absolute expiry timestamp, reject expired rows on resolve, and filter the returned document by the recorded scopes.

reported.title: TOCTOU between existence check and open() widened by a 200ms sleep
reported.body: `export_document` checks `os.path.exists(destination)`, then deliberately sleeps 200ms, then opens the path with mode `"w"`, which truncates. Two concurrent exports of the same filename both pass the existence check and the second silently overwrites the first; more seriously, anything created at that path during the sleep window (including a symlink planted in the shared export root) is truncated and overwritten. Store an absolute expiry (`time.time() + ttl`) and reject resolved rows whose expiry is in the past. The scopes stored on the share are likewise ignored when the document is returned.

reported.title: Remote import reads an unbounded response body into memory
reported.body: `response.text` buffers the entire remote body with no size limit. Because the URL is caller-supplied (`handle_import_url`), a user can point the importer at a multi-gigabyte or endless stream and exhaust the server's memory; the request timeout only bounds the time to first byte/connection, not total transfer size. Stream the response and abort once a maximum byte count is exceeded.

survived.title: Admin check in purge_user is swallowed by bare except
survived.body: `_assert_admin(user)` raises `Forbidden` for non-admins, but the call is wrapped in `try/except Exception: pass`, so the failure is discarded and execution continues to the `DELETE FROM documents WHERE owner_id = ?` statement. Any authenticated (non-admin) caller who reaches `purge_user` can delete every document belonging to an arbitrary `target_user_id`. A check that fails silently is equivalent to no check.

survived.title: delete_document performs no authorization check
survived.body: `delete_document` is reachable from `handle_delete_document`, which only calls `auth.require_user(token)`. It never calls `_assert_admin` and never verifies that the caller owns the document — it deletes any row by id. Any authenticated user can therefore destroy any other user's documents by guessing/iterating `doc_id`. The `_assert_admin` helper defined immediately above is simply never used here.

survived.title: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded development value
survived.body: `SECRET_KEY` now defaults to the literal `"dev-secret-change-me"` when `QUORUM_DEMO_SECRET` is unset. This key signs share links (`sharing.sign`), so a deployment that forgets the environment variable silently runs with a publicly known signing key and anyone can forge a valid share signature for any `doc_id`. The previous `os.environ[...]` lookup failed fast at import time, which is the correct behaviour for a signing key.

survived.title: Page-size clamp removed from list_documents
survived.body: The `min(int(limit), Config.MAX_PAGE_SIZE)` clamp was dropped, so `handle_list_documents(token, limit=10_000_000)` now issues an unbounded query and materialises every matching row into a list of dicts. A single authenticated request can exhaust memory on the server. `Config.MAX_PAGE_SIZE` still exists and is now unused.

survived.title: Path traversal: export filename joined without validation
survived.body: `export_path` joins the caller-supplied `filename` onto the user's export directory with no normalisation or containment check, and `export_document` (exposed via `handle_export`) then opens the result with mode `"w"`. A filename such as `../../etc/cron.d/job` or `../<other-user-id>/report.json` escapes the caller's directory and overwrites arbitrary files the process can write; an absolute path like `/etc/passwd` bypasses the join entirely because `os.path.join` discards the prefix. Note that `indexer.extract_text` performs exactly the `realpath` + `commonpath` containment check that is missing here, and `reports.write_report` sanitises through `validators.export_name`; `export_path` should do the same.

survived.title: SQL injection: search term interpolated into query string
survived.body: `search()` builds the SQL with an f-string, embedding the caller-supplied `term` (and `user["id"]`) directly into the statement. A term containing a single quote terminates the literal, e.g. `term = "x' OR 1=1 --"` returns every row regardless of `owner_id`, and on SQLite backends that allow multiple statements the same input can be used to read or modify other tables. `db.query` clearly supports bound parameters (see `suggest()` below), so this is avoidable. The `column` value is already constrained by the `SORTABLE` allowlist, but `term` and the owner id are not.

survived.title: SSRF: user-supplied URL fetched with no scheme or host allowlist
survived.body: `fetch_remote_document` passes the caller's raw `url` straight to `requests.get`, and it is exposed through `handle_import_url`. Any authenticated user can make the server issue requests to internal addresses — e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` on EC2, `http://metadata.google.internal/...` on GCP, or `http://127.0.0.1:*` internal admin ports — and the response body is returned to them verbatim as `body`. `file://` and other schemes supported by installed adapters are equally reachable, and redirects are followed by default. The URL must be validated: restrict the scheme to http/https, resolve the host and reject private/loopback/link-local addresses, and disable redirects (or re-validate each hop).

survived.title: Mutable default argument leaks scopes between share links
survived.body: `scopes: list = []` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every caller that omits `scopes` shares the same list object. The body mutates it via `scopes.append("read")`, and `handle_create_share` passes caller-supplied lists through on the other branch. After the first default call the shared list permanently contains `"read"`, and any future mutation of that object (e.g. a caller that holds the returned `scopes` list from the response dict and appends to it) is visible to every subsequent default-argument share link — escalating the privileges granted by later links.

survived.title: TOCTOU between existence check and write in export_document
survived.body: The code checks `os.path.exists(destination)`, then sleeps 200 ms, then opens the path with mode `"w"`, which truncates. Anything that creates the file during that window — a concurrent export request from the same user, or a symlink planted by another local process — is silently overwritten, defeating the `FileExistsError` guard. Opening with mode `"x"` makes the check and the create a single atomic operation.

survived.title: Share signature compared with non-constant-time !=
survived.body: `resolve_share_link` compares the recomputed signature against the client-supplied one with `!=`. Python's string comparison short-circuits on the first differing byte, so response timing leaks how many leading bytes of a guessed signature are correct, allowing an attacker to recover a valid signature byte by byte without knowing `SECRET_KEY`. Use `hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature)` instead (requires `import hmac` at the top of the module).

survived.title: Share link expiry is stored but never enforced
survived.body: `expires_at` is set to the raw TTL (`ttl or DEFAULT_TTL_SECONDS`) rather than an absolute timestamp, and it is written into the `expires_in` column. `resolve_share_link` selects only `doc_id, scopes` and never reads or checks that column, so every share link is valid forever — the advertised 7-day TTL has no effect. Store an absolute expiry (`time.time() + ttl`) and reject resolved rows whose expiry is in the past. The scopes stored on the share are likewise ignored when the document is returned.
